paragraphs.text: The divine apostle always speaks with a divine and heavenly tongue, and weaves the message of the gospel with great skill. He does not simply speak from his own opinion; he sets forth his teachings on the authority of the King himself. But he uses this skill above all when he brings the message of repentance to sinners, and it is on this very subject that I want to remind you all. You heard just now, to touch on part of what was read, how that noble and wonderful man said, as he addressed the Corinthians: "I fear that when I come I may have to mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." This great teacher was a man by nature but a servant of God by choice. That is why he speaks, as it were, with a heavenly tongue, and as though speaking from heaven itself he threatens sinners and promises atonement to those who repent. When I say this, I am not ascribing the authority to Paul's tongue. I attribute the whole of it to the grace of God, of which he himself said just now: "Since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me." So he offers sinners a healing remedy, and repentance that leads to salvation. Today the Savior's own authority in the Gospel has joined the reading from the apostle, freely granting forgiveness of sins. For as you have just heard, when the Savior healed the paralytic he said: "Child, your many sins are forgiven." Forgiveness of sins is a fountain of salvation and the prize of repentance. Repentance is a medicine that destroys sin. It is a heavenly gift and a wonderful power, which by grace overcomes the strict course of the laws. That is why it does not shake off the fornicator, does not drive away the adulterer, does not turn away from the drunkard, does not loathe the idolater, does not banish the slanderer, and does not chase away the blasphemer or the boaster. Instead, it transforms them all. Repentance is a furnace in which sin is melted down. But first we must understand God's purpose. We should not approach this subject from our own ideas but show the truth as the divine Scriptures themselves bear witness to it. God's purpose is to be patient with sinners. His mercy toward salvation is twofold: he woos them toward the salvation that comes through repentance, and he stores up his kindness for those of their descendants who will advance in virtue. To restate the point: God is patient so that the sinner may repent, and so that he may not shut off salvation from those born of him. Even if the sinner himself keeps offending without repenting, God often spares the root in order to preserve the fruit. Often, as I said before, he transforms the root itself. But when the root falls into utter wickedness, God wisely postpones the punishment and waits for the salvation of those who will repent. Listen to how this works. Terah, the father of Abraham, worshiped idols, yet he did not pay the penalty for his impiety in this life, and rightly so. If God had cut off the root beforehand, where would so great a fruit of faith have come from? What was more wicked than Esau? Look with me at another example of God's love for mankind. What was more shameless than that man's wickedness? Was he not a fornicator and profane, as the apostle says? Did he not strike his mother and his father? Was he not his brother's murderer, at least in intention? Was he not hated by God? Scripture bears witness when it says: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." If he was a fornicator, a fratricide, profane, and hated, why is he not destroyed? Why is he not cut down? Why does he not receive the punishment he deserves at once? Why? It is good to state the reason plainly. If he had been cut down, the world would have lost a very great fruit of righteousness. Listen to what that fruit was. Esau fathered Reuel, Reuel fathered Zerah, and Zerah fathered Jobab. Do you see what a great flower of endurance would have been destroyed if God had punished the root beforehand?

So apply this principle to everything. This is why he is patient with the Egyptians, though their blasphemies were unbearable: because of the churches that now flourish in Egypt, because of the monasteries, and because of those who have taken up the angelic life. Those who are experienced in the common law say, and the laws of the Romans direct, that if a pregnant woman ever commits an offense that carries the death penalty, she is not to be executed until she has given birth to the child she is carrying. This is quite right, for those who wisely framed the laws did not think it just that the innocent should perish together with the woman who sinned. If human laws spare those who have done nothing wrong, will God not have much more reason to preserve the root, storing up the kindness of repentance for its fruit? Now consider with me the kindness of repentance toward sinners themselves, for the same principle of God's love for mankind applies to them too. If punishment came before correction, the world would have perished and been destroyed completely. If God were quick to punish, the church would not have gained Paul and would never have received so great a man. That is why God bore with him while he blasphemed, so that he could show him repenting. God's patience made the persecutor a preacher. God's patience changed the wolf into a shepherd. God's patience made the tax collector an evangelist. God's patience has had mercy on us all, changed us all, and turned us all back. If you see a former drunkard fasting, a former blasphemer speaking of God, or someone who once defiled his mouth with shameful songs now purifying his soul with divine hymns, marvel at God's patience and praise repentance. Then take up the words of Scripture and say of the change: "This change is the work of the right hand of the Most High." God is good to all, but he shows his patience especially toward sinners. If you want to hear a strange saying, listen. It is strange by the standards of custom but true by the standards of piety.

Everywhere God appears stern toward the righteous but kind toward sinners and quick to show his love for mankind. He raises up the one who has sinned and fallen, and says to him: "Does the one who falls not get up again? Does the one who turns away not turn back?" He also says: "Why has the foolish daughter of Judah turned away so shamelessly?" And again: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you." Elsewhere, in his great love for mankind, he confirms with an oath that salvation comes through repentance: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner; I desire that he turn and live." But to the righteous he says: "If a man does all that is righteous and all that is true, and then turns and sins, I will not remember his righteousness; he will die in his sin." How strict he is with the righteous! How generous he is with the sinner! He works in these varied and different ways without changing himself. He wisely apportions the dispensations of his goodness. Listen to how this works. If he frightens a sinner who persists in his sins, he drives him to despair and makes him give up hope. But if he calls the righteous man blessed, he slackens the tension of his virtue and leads him to neglect his effort, as though he were already blessed. That is why he has mercy on the sinner but frightens the righteous: "For he is to be feared by all who are around him," and "The Lord is kind to all." Scripture says he is to be feared by all who are around him. Who could these be but the saints? "For God," says David, "who is glorified in the council of the saints, is great and to be feared by all who are around him." If he sees someone who has fallen, he stretches out a hand of love. If he sees someone standing, he instills fear in him. This too is a mark of righteousness and just judgment, for he steadies the righteous with fear and rouses the sinner with love. Do you want to know how timely his goodness is, and how useful and fitting his severity is for us? Pay close attention, so that the greatness of what we are considering does not escape you. There was a sinful woman, notorious for every sin and lawless deed. She had sinned so much and was entangled in so many sinful acts, yet she thirsted for the salvation that comes through repentance, and she slipped into the banquet of the saints. I call it a banquet of saints because the Holy One of the holy ones was present. While the Savior was reclining at table in the house of Simon the Pharisee, that sinful woman slipped in and took hold of the Savior's feet. She washed his feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. And the Lover of mankind raised up this woman, who was buried under so many sins, saying: "Her sins are forgiven." It is not my aim now to examine the whole story, only to bring forward the testimony. See how generous he is: "Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much." So the sinful woman received amnesty for all those sins. Yet Miriam, the sister of Moses, is condemned to leprosy for a little grumbling. To sinners he says: "Though your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow." He turns darkness into light through the change that repentance brings, and he dissolves so great an abundance of evils with the voice of his goodness. But to the one who walks in righteousness he says: "Whoever says to his brother, 'You fool,' is liable to the fire of Gehenna." He attached such strictness to a single word, yet he measures out such abundant mercy for so many sins.

Consider with me another marvel. Sins are recorded as debts. From sinners who repent he forgives even the principal, but from the righteous he demands interest as well. A man who owed many talents came to him, and by repentance and much pleading he softened the sentence, saying: "Lord, be patient with me, and I will repay everything." The Lover of mankind did not wait to be repaid. He made the man's confession the cancellation of the debt. He forgave the debtor of ten thousand talents everything, even the principal itself. But from the righteous he declares that he will demand interest as well: "Why did you not give my money to the bankers, so that when I came I could have collected it with interest?" I do not say this as though God were hostile to the righteous, for nothing is dearer to God than a righteous man. As I said before, he comforts the sinner in order to rouse him, and he frightens the righteous in order to steady him. He forgives many offenses to the one group, as to enemies and to the puffed up, but he is exacting with the other group even about trifles, because he wants them to lack nothing in reaching perfection. What a rich man is in this world, the righteous man is to God, and what a poor man is in this world, the sinner is to God. Nothing is poorer than one who sins, and nothing is richer than one who does what is right. That is why Paul says of those who live in piety and abundance: "I thank God that in every way you have been enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge." But of the impious the blessed Jeremiah says: "Perhaps they are poor; that is why they could not hear the word of the Lord." You see how he calls those who are cut off from piety poor. He pities sinners as poor, and he makes demands of those who do right as rich. He is gracious to the one group because of their poverty, and from the other, because of their wealth in piety, he exacts the accounts with great strictness. What he does with the righteous and with sinners, he also does with the rich and the poor. He raises up the sinner through his love for mankind and frightens the righteous by his severity, and in the same way he orders his dispensation in worldly affairs. If he sees powerful men who shine with high rank, such as kings, rulers, and all who are distinguished by wealth, he speaks to them with fear, and he wisely lays fear upon their power: "And now, you kings, understand; be instructed, all you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling." For "he is King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule." Where there is the rule of power, he imposes the fear of his own kingship. Where there is the humility of lowliness, he offers the remedy of his love. This God is the great King of kings and Lord of lords. Yet this same God, stepping down from his dignity, is found according to holy Scripture to be "a father of orphans and a judge for widows": King of kings, Ruler of rulers, Lord of lords. Do you see the great abundance of his love? Do you see how useful the fear of piety and of his authority is? Where he saw that power was enough comfort in itself, he added fear for their benefit. But where he saw orphans enfeebled by their lowliness, and poverty enfeebled by the helplessness of widowhood, he brought his love to comfort them. "I am the father of orphans." He does two things: he shows his love for mankind and he restrains power. He calls himself the father of orphans in order to comfort those in misfortune and to strike terror into those in power, so that they will not mistreat orphans and widows. Death had stripped the one of his father and robbed the other of her husband, but those whom the law of nature had ruined, the decree of his love renewed. The same grace gave the widow a judge and the orphan a father: the King of the saints. "So then," he says, "you unjust man, if you mistreat widows, you provoke the protector of widows. If you wrong orphans, you wrong the sons of God." "I am the father of orphans and the judge of widows." Who is so bold in impiety as to wrong the sons of God and mistreat the widows God cares for? Do you see how wisely he prepares the remedies of piety? He frightens some and pities others. He is not divided in himself; he adapts himself to the dispositions of men. Let us then apply repentance to ourselves, brothers, as a remedy for salvation. Or rather, let us receive from God the repentance that heals us. We do not offer it to him; he has supplied it to us. Do you see his strictness under the law? Do you see his love for mankind under grace? When I speak of the strictness under the law, I am not finding fault with judgment. I am proclaiming the love of the grace of the gospel. The law punished sinners without mercy, but grace patiently postpones the punishment in order to bring about correction. So let us accept repentance, brothers, as a remedy for salvation. Let us accept a remedy that wipes out our offenses. True repentance is not proclaimed in words but confirmed by deeds. It is repentance that wipes out the filth of impiety from the heart itself. "Wash yourselves," Scripture says, "make yourselves clean; remove the wickedness from your hearts before my eyes." What is the point of the extra words? Is "Remove the wickedness from your hearts" not enough to say it all? Why then add "before my eyes"? Because human eyes see in one way and the eye of God sees in another: "For man looks on the face, but God looks on the heart." He is saying: "Do not counterfeit repentance with outward shows. Show the fruits of repentance before my eyes, which search out what is hidden."

As we are being cleansed of our sins, we must keep the sins themselves before our eyes. Even if God in his love for mankind forgives you your sin, you should still keep that sin before your eyes for the safety of your own soul. Remembering past sins acts as a check on future ones, and anyone who feels the sting of his earlier sins shows a firmer resolve against the next ones. That is why David also says: "My sin is always before me." By keeping the past before his eyes, he would not fall into future sins. And to see that God requires this disposition of us, listen to what he says: "I am the one who blots out your sins, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us argue our case, says the Lord. State your sins first, so that you may be justified." God does not wait for time to pass after repentance. You confessed your sin, and you were justified. You repented, and you received mercy. It is not the length of time that makes the defense. It is the manner of the penitent that quenches the sin. A person can persist for a long time and still fail to obtain salvation, and another can confess sincerely in a short time and strip off his sin. The blessed Samuel spent a long time pleading for Saul and passed many sleepless nights over the salvation of the man who had sinned. But God disregarded the time, because the sinner's repentance did not go along with the prophet's pleading, and he said to his prophet: "How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?" "How long" points to the time and to the persistence of the one who was pleading. God disregarded the time the prophet spent pleading, because the king's repentance did not go along with the righteous man's intercession. But blessed David received the rebuke for his sin through the holy prophet Nathan, and at once, in response to the threat, he showed sincere conversion and said: "I have sinned against the Lord." At once a single word, spoken sincerely in a single moment, brought complete salvation to the penitent. His correction immediately overtook the sentence. So Nathan says to him: "And the Lord has taken away your sin."

See how God is slow to punish and quick to save. First consider how the Lover of mankind brought the rebuke only after a long time. David sinned and the woman conceived, but no rebuke followed the sin. Only after the child born of the sin was delivered was the physician of the sin sent. Why did God not correct him immediately after he sinned? Because he knows that when sin is at its height the soul of the sinner is blind, and the ears of those plunged in the depths of sin are deaf. So he holds back from bringing help while the passion is still inflamed. The rebuke comes after a long time, and repentance and forgiveness happen in a single moment: "And the Lord has taken away your sin." How wise is the dispensation of the one who threatened! Do you see that he is quick to save? He does the same with others: he is slow to destroy and quick to help. Here is what I mean. Among us humans, buildings take a long time to construct, and it takes a long time to build a house. Building takes a long time, but demolishing takes very little. With God it is the reverse. When he builds, he builds quickly. When he overthrows, he overthrows slowly. God is quick to build and slow to overthrow, because both befit God: the first shows his power, and the second shows his goodness. He is quick because of his surpassing power and slow because of his great goodness. The facts themselves prove what I am saying. In six days God made heaven and earth, the great mountains, the plains, the ravines, the glens, the forests, the plants, the springs, the rivers, paradise, all the variety we see, "this sea, great and wide," the islands, and the coastal and inland lands. God made this whole visible world and all its beauty in six days. In six days he makes the living creatures in it, both rational and irrational, and all the visible order. Yet this God who is so quick to create was found to be slow, because of his goodness, when he resolved to bring down a single city. He wants to bring down Jericho, and he says to Israel: "March around it for seven days, and on the seventh day the wall will fall." You fashion the whole world in six days, yet you take seven days to destroy one city? What hinders your might? Why do you not bring it down all at once? Is it not of you that the prophet cries out: "If you open the heavens, the mountains will tremble at you and melt like wax before the fire"? Does not David say, as he recounts the works of your power: "We will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas"? You can move mountains and cast them into the sea, yet you do not want to bring down one city that resists you, but give seven days to its destruction? Why? "It is not that my power is weak," he says, "but that my love for mankind is patient. I give seven days, as I gave Nineveh three days. Perhaps it will accept the preaching of repentance and be saved." And who was preaching repentance to them? Enemies had surrounded the city. The general was marching around the walls. There was great fear and great turmoil. What way of repentance did you open to them? Did you send a prophet? Did you dispatch an evangelist? Was there anyone to advise them about what was good for them? "Yes," he says, "they had a teacher of repentance inside the city: that wonderful Rahab, whom I saved through repentance. She was made of the same clay as they were. But because she did not share their way of thinking, she who had no share in their unbelief had no share in their sin."

And see, I pray you, how strange this proclamation of loving-kindness is. He who says in the law, "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit fornication," changes his word out of love for humankind and cries out through the blessed Joshua, "Let Rahab the harlot live." That Joshua, the son of Nun, who said, "Let the harlot live," was an image of the Lord Jesus, who says, "Harlots and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of heaven." If she ought to live, why call her "harlot"? If she is a harlot, why "let her live"? I mention her former condition, he says, so that you may marvel at her second transformation. "And what," someone asks, "did Rahab do to win salvation? Receive the spies in peace? An innkeeper does that too." But she does not gain salvation from the bare word [?] alone. It comes first of all from her faith and her disposition toward God. And so that you may learn how surpassing her faith was, listen to Scripture itself recounting the achievements it attests of her. She was in a brothel, like a pearl mixed into mire, gold scattered in mud, a flower of piety buried among thorns: a pious soul shut up in a place of impiety. Now pay close attention, I pray you. She received the spies, and the One whom Israel betrayed in the wilderness, Rahab proclaimed in the brothel. What do I mean by Israel in the wilderness? When the mountain was filled with cloud and darkness and trumpets and lightnings and all the other terrors, Israel heard God speak from the midst of the fire: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one. You shall have no other gods. I am in heaven above and on the earth below, and besides me there is no God." Israel heard this, then cast a calf and set God aside. They ignored their Master, renounced their Benefactor, and said to Aaron, "Make us gods." If they are gods, why "make"? How can things that are made be gods? So wickedness, in its blindness, fights against itself and destroys itself.

"These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." "These are the gods." They see one calf; the idol that was made is one. Why then "These are the gods"? To show that they worship more than what they see: they imagine a multitude of gods. The words express their intention; they do not describe what appears. But to return to our subject: the very things that Israel heard and denied, Israel surrounded by so many wonders and schooled by such a law, Rahab proclaims, shut up in the brothel. For she says to the spies, "We know all that your God did to the Egyptians." The Jew says, "These are your gods who brought you out of the land of Egypt," but the harlot ascribes the deliverance not to gods but to God. "We know all that your God did to the Egyptians in the wilderness. We heard it, and our hearts melted, and there is no strength left in us." "We know all that your God did." Do you see how through faith she takes up the lawgiver's very words? "And I know that your God is in heaven above and on the earth below, and besides him there is no God."

Rahab is an image of the Church. The Church was once defiled by fornication with demons, but now it receives the spies of Christ: not the ones sent by Joshua son of Nun, but the apostles sent by Jesus, the true Savior. "I know," she says, "that your God is in heaven above and on the earth below, and besides him there is no God." The Jews received this and did not keep it; the Church heard it and kept it faithfully. Rahab, then, the image of the Church, is worthy of all praise. That is why the noble Paul also numbers her among all the saints. He understood the worth of her faith, and he did not count her unworthy because of her former state but approved because of her God-given change. He said, "By faith Abel offered a sacrifice; by faith Abraham did this and that; by faith Noah built an ark; by faith Moses did and achieved this and that," and went on to mention many saints in turn. Then at the last he added, "By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who disobeyed, because she received the spies and sent them out by another way." And see with what great wisdom she tempered her goodwill. When men were sent by the king to look for the spies, they said to her, "Did some men come in to you?" And she said to them, "Yes, they came." First she lays a foundation of truth, and only then does she add the lie. For a lie is never believed on its own unless it first shows some truth. That is why those who lie persuasively first say what is true and admitted by everyone, and then add what is false and open to doubt. "Did spies come in to you?" She says yes. Had she said no from the start, she would have provoked the men who came to search. Instead she says, "They came in, and they went out by this road. Pursue them, and you will overtake them." O fine lie! O fine deceit, which did not betray the things of God but guarded piety! If repentance made that Rahab worthy of such salvation, and the mouths of saints proclaim her, with Joshua son of Nun crying out in the wilderness, "Let Rahab the harlot live," and Paul saying, "By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with those who disobeyed," how much more shall we receive salvation if we offer repentance? Now is the time for repentance. Great is the dread of the sins that weigh upon us, unless repentance forestalls the punishment. "Let us come before his face with confession." Let us quench the blaze of our sins, not with much water but with a few tears. The fire of sin is great, yet a little tear quenches it, for a tear puts out the blaze of sins and washes away the stench of sin. The blessed David bears witness to this, saying and showing how great the power of tears is: "Every night I will bathe my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch." Yet if he had only wanted to show how abundant his tears were, it would have been enough to say, "With my tears I will drench my couch." Why then did he put "I will bathe" first? To show that tears are a bath and a cleansing from sins.

Sins are the cause of all evils. Because of sins come griefs; because of sins, disturbances; because of sins, wars; because of sins, diseases, and all the hard-to-cure afflictions that befall us. The best physicians do not examine only the visible symptoms; they seek the cause of what appears. In the same way the Savior wished to show that sin is the cause of all human evils, so he speaks to the man paralyzed in body. Since the Physician of souls saw that he had been paralyzed first in soul and only then in body, he says to him, "See, you have been made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." So sin was the cause of his earlier sickness as well. Sin is the cause of loss; it becomes the source of grief and of every misfortune. But this is what I marvel at: God gave grief to man from the beginning because of sin, yet he undoes the sentence by means of the sentence and drives out the condemnation by means of the condemnation. Grief was given because of sin, and through grief sin is undone. Pay close attention. When God threatened the woman and imposed the punishment for her transgression, he said to her, "In grief you shall bear children," and so showed that grief is the fruit of sin. But O the generosity of the Giver! What he gave as punishment he turned into salvation. Sin gave birth to grief, and grief consumed sin. A worm born from wood eats up that very wood; so too grief, born from sin, consumes sin when it is offered through repentance. That is why Paul says, "Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." Grief is good for those who truly repent, and mourning over sin befits sinners: "For blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." Mourn your sin, so that you will not have to lament your punishment. Make your defense to the Judge before you come to the tribunal. Or do you not know that people who want to win a judge over do not court him during the actual hearing of the case? Before they enter the court, they court the judge through friends or patrons or by some other means. So it is with God as well: once the judgment seat is set, the Judge cannot be persuaded, but before the time of judgment he can be won over. That is why David said, "Let us come before his face with confession." There, the great Judge is not deceived by the orators' art. Power does not sway him; rank does not persuade him; he shows no deference to anyone's person; money does not corrupt him. His righteous judgment is fearful and inexorable.

Here, then, let us win over the Judge and entreat him. Here let us beseech him with all our strength, though not with money. Or rather, if the truth must be told, the Lover of mankind is persuaded even by money. He does not receive it himself; he receives it through the poor. Give money to someone in need, and you have won over the Judge. I say this to win you to my side, since repentance without almsgiving is dead and wingless. Repentance cannot take flight if it lacks the wing of almsgiving. That is why, for Cornelius, who repented well, almsgiving became the wing of his piety: "Your alms and your prayers," it says, "have gone up to heaven." It is as if repentance would not have reached heaven had it not had almsgiving for a wing. So today a market for almsgiving has opened. We see the captives and the poor; we see those carried about in the marketplace; we see those crying out, those weeping, those groaning. A wonderful fair lies before us. A fair has no other purpose, and a merchant no other aim, than to buy goods cheap and sell them dear. Is this not every merchant's goal? Does anyone take up trade for any other reason than to sell dear what he bought cheap and to carry off his stock multiplied? Such is the fair God has set before us. Buy righteous deeds cheaply, so that you may resell them dear in the age to come, if the recompense may be called a resale. Here righteousness is bought for little: for a cheap scrap of bread, a cheap garment, a cup of cold water. "Whoever gives a cup of cold water to drink, truly I tell you," says the teacher of spiritual trade, "will by no means lose his reward." If a cup of cold water earns a reward, do garments and money given in kindness not earn one? On the contrary, they earn a great one. Why then did he mention a cup of cold water? He was speaking of almsgiving that costs nothing, for with cold water you burn no wood and spend nothing else. If the favor shown to a kindness is so great where the gift costs nothing, how great a reward should we expect from the just Judge where there is an abundance of garments, a supply of money, a wealth of other goods? So while the virtues are set out for sale at a low price, let us take them from the generous Giver; let us seize them, let us buy them. "You who thirst," it says, "come to the water, and you who have no money, go and buy." While the fair is on, let us buy almsgiving, or rather, through almsgiving let us buy salvation. When you clothe a poor man, you clothe Christ. "I know this well and exactly," someone says. "I learned it long ago. You are not the first to teach it, and we did not first hear it from you. You are preaching nothing new, only what many of those here have often taught us." I know it myself, I know that you have often learned these things and others like them. But would that, having learned them so often, we might do even a little good. "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God." Let us lend our almsgiving to God, so that we may receive from him loving-kindness in return. O most wise saying! "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God." Why did it not say, "Whoever has mercy on the poor gives to God," but "lends"? Scripture knows our greed. It saw that our insatiable appetite, with its eye on gain, looks for interest. That is why it did not say simply, "Whoever has mercy on the poor gives to God," lest you think the repayment would be no more than what you gave. It said, "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God." If God borrows from us, then he is our debtor. Which, then, do you want him to be, judge or debtor? A debtor shows respect to the one who lent to him; a judge shows no deference to a borrower.

We must also look at another reason why God said, "The one who gives to the poor lends to me." He saw, as I said before, that our greed leans toward interest, and that no one with money is ever willing to lend without security. The lender demands a mortgage, or pledges, or a guarantor, and only on these three securities does he entrust his money, accepting sureties, as I said, or a mortgage on property, or pledges. God saw that apart from these no one lends; no one looks to kindness, only to profit. And the poor man has none of these things. He has no mortgage to offer, for he owns nothing. He brings no pledges, for he has been stripped bare. He provides no guarantor, for his poverty makes him distrusted. So when God saw the poor man in peril from his poverty, and the man with money in peril through his inhumanity, he put himself between them, a surety for the poor man and a pledge for the lender. "You distrust this man," he says, "because of his poverty; trust me because of my abundance." He saw the poor man and had mercy. He saw the poor man and did not overlook him, but gave himself as a pledge for the one who had nothing, and in his great goodness stood beside the needy. The blessed David confirms this loving-kindness when he says, "For he stood at the right hand of the poor." "Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God." "Take heart," he says, "you are lending to me." "And what do I gain by lending to you?" To demand an account from God is, to be sure, utterly lawless. Still, so that I may stoop to your lawlessness and undo strictness with loving-kindness, let us compare the two. When you lend to others, what do you gain? What interest do you seek from them? Is it not one per cent, if you ask the legal rate? But if your greed grows, you will reap twice and three times as much injustice. "I, however, outdo your greed. I surpass your insatiable craving. I cover your excess with my abundance. You seek one in a hundred, but I give you a hundredfold." "So you borrow, Lord. You borrow from me here the alms given to the poor. When will you repay me? I demand the terms of the agreement, because I want to secure the contract. Give me the date of repayment; set the deadline for recovering my loan." This is, in truth, superfluous, for "the Lord is faithful in all his words." But since it is the custom and concern of a prudent lender to measure out periods and fix days, hear when and where the One who borrowed through the poor man repays you the debt. "When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory, and sets the sheep on his right and the goats on his left, he will say to those on his right…" Here notice how grateful the debtor is to the lender, how graciously the borrower repays: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." For what? "For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me; I was in prison and you came to me; I was sick and you visited me; I was a stranger and you took me in." Then those who served well in due season look at their own weakness and at the dignity of the Borrower, and they say, "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink?" You, on whom the eyes of all hope, who give them their food in abundance? O great goodness! He hides his dignity out of loving-kindness: "For I was hungry and you gave me food." O great goodness, O measureless kindness! He who gives food to all flesh, who opens his hands and fills every living thing with his good pleasure, says, "I was hungry and you gave me food." His dignity is not diminished by this; rather, his loving-kindness stands surety for the poor. "I was thirsty and you gave me drink." Who says this? He who pours out water in lakes and rivers and springs; he who says through the Gospels, "Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water"; he who said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Yet he says, "I was naked and you clothed me." Did we clothe the One who clothes the heaven with clouds, who clothes the whole Church and the whole world? "For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." "I was in prison." You in prison, who lead out those in fetters? Explain what you are saying, for your dignity contradicts your words. When did we see you in such need? When did we do these things? "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these," he says, "you did it to me." Is the saying not true, then, that "whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God"? And see the marvel: he mentioned no other work of virtue but this. He could have said, "Come, you blessed, because you lived chastely, because you kept your virginity, because you took up the angelic life." But he says nothing of these, not because they are unworthy of mention but because they rank below loving-kindness. He showed that the kingdom was granted to those on the right because of their loving-kindness, and in the same way he threatened those on the left with punishment because they bore no fruit. "Depart, you cursed, into the outer darkness prepared for the devil and his angels." Why? For what? "Because I was hungry and you gave me no food." He did not say, "Because you committed fornication, because you committed adultery, because you stole, because you bore false witness, because you swore falsely." These too are evils, admittedly, but they rank below inhumanity and mercilessness. But why, O Lord, do you make no mention of other ways? "I do not judge sin," he says, "but inhumanity. I do not judge those who sinned, but those who did not repent. I condemn you for inhumanity, because you had almsgiving, so great and so mighty a remedy for salvation, by which all your sins would have been blotted out, and you neglected so great a benefit. So I reproach inhumanity as the root of wickedness and of all impiety, and I praise loving-kindness as the root of all good things. To the one group I threaten eternal fire; to the other I promise the kingdom of heaven." Good, O Master, are your promises. Good is the kingdom we hope for, and good too is the Gehenna you threaten: the one spurs us on, the other frightens us. The kingdom spurs us on to good effect, and Gehenna frightens us to our profit. For God threatens Gehenna not to cast us into it but to deliver us from it. If he wished to punish, he would not have threatened us beforehand so that we might secure ourselves and escape what he threatens. He threatens punishment so that we may escape the experience of punishment; he frightens us with a word so that he need not punish us in deed. Let us therefore lend our loving-kindness to God. Let us lend, so that we may find him a debtor, as I said before, and not a judge. For a debtor respects his lender; he respects him and is abashed before him. If a lender goes to a debtor's door, the debtor runs away if he has no means; but if he is well off, he welcomes him with confidence. And see, I pray you, another marvel of the just Judge, set beside human ways. Suppose you lend to someone who is in poverty, and the borrower comes into prosperity and is now able to repay you the debt. He repays it without letting most people know, so as not to be shamed over his former condition. He acknowledges his gratitude, but he hides the kindness, because he is ashamed of his former need. God does not do so. He borrows in secret, but he repays the debt openly. When he receives, it is through almsgiving done in secret; but when he repays, he repays before the eyes of all creation. But perhaps someone will say, "Why did he not give to the poor man just as he gave to me, the rich man?" He could have given to you and to the poor man alike, but he did not want your wealth to be fruitless or the poor man's poverty to go unrewarded. To you, the rich man, he has granted to be rich in almsgiving and to scatter in righteousness: "For he has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever." Do you see that the rich man stores up eternal righteousness through almsgiving? Look again at the poor man. Since he has no wealth with which to work righteousness, he has poverty, and from it he reaps eternal patience: "For the patience of the poor shall not perish forever," in Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
